stories.headline: U.S. MARKETS DARK FOR JUNETEENTH; QUOTES HELD FROM THURSDAY'S CLOSE
stories.body: The NYSE, Nasdaq and the bond market are closed for the Juneteenth federal holiday, giving investors a three-day weekend. The strip above reflects Thursday's June 18 levels; normal trading resumes Monday, June 22.
stories.explain: Exchange holidays freeze price discovery, so there is no fresh print to react to today. The carried-over numbers show a market that bounced Thursday (S&P +1.08%, NDX +2.48%) after Wednesday's hawkish-Fed selloff, leaving the week's tone still defined by Wednesday's decision rather than Thursday's relief rally.

stories.headline: WARSH FED HOLDS AT 3.50%-3.75% AND SCRAPS THE 2026 RATE CUT
stories.body: At Wednesday's meeting the FOMC under new Chair Kevin Warsh left the funds rate unchanged and removed the lone 2026 cut from the dot plot; 9 of 18 officials now pencil in at least one more hike to fight sticky inflation.
stories.explain: Pricing out a cut and adding hike risk lifts the expected path of short rates, which is why the 2-year yield pushed to ~4.20% even as the 10-year sat near 4.44%. A higher-for-longer policy rate raises the discount rate on equities and is the proximate cause of Wednesday's drawdown.

stories.headline: WTI NEAR $74.62, ON TRACK FOR A ROUGHLY 10% WEEKLY LOSS
stories.body: Crude slid as planned U.S.-Iran talks in Switzerland were canceled but feared supply disruptions failed to materialize, with WTI down about 4% Thursday and roughly 10% on the week.
stories.explain: A geopolitical risk premium built into oil earlier this month is bleeding out as Hormuz stays open and barrels keep flowing. Falling energy prices ease one inflation input, a modest offset to the Fed's hawkishness, but also signal markets pricing softer global demand.

stories.headline: DOLLAR AT A TWO-MONTH HIGH NEAR 100.7 KEEPS GOLD ON THE BACK FOOT
stories.body: The DXY firmed to roughly 100.7, its best level in two months, as the hawkish Fed repricing widened the U.S. rate advantage; gold eased to about $4,209.
stories.explain: Gold pays no coupon, so higher real yields and a stronger dollar raise its opportunity cost and weigh on the price. The same hawkish shift that lifted the 2-year yield is simultaneously bullish for the dollar and bearish for bullion, a textbook rate-driven rotation playing out in real time.

stories.headline: JUST 71 EARLY ENTRANTS FOR 2026 DRAFT, FEWEST IN TWO DECADES
stories.body: NIL money pulled stars back to campus: only 71 players filed as early entrants, headlined by freshmen AJ Dybantsa (BYU), Darryn Peterson (Kansas) and Cameron Boozer (Duke). The draft runs June 23-24 at Barclays Center.

stories.headline: KNICKS WIN FIRST TITLE IN 53 YEARS, BEAT SPURS 4-1
stories.body: New York closed out San Antonio to capture its first championship since 1973 and paraded down the Canyon of Heroes on June 18. The offseason now turns to the June 23-24 draft and free agency.

stories.headline: BLOCKBUSTER TRADES RESHAPE ROSTERS AS MINICAMPS WRAP
stories.body: A June 1 swap sent Myles Garrett from Cleveland to the Rams and A.J. Brown to the Patriots; the Falcons later added Chiefs tackle Wanya Morris. Teams are signing undrafted rookies with training camps under two months away.

stories.headline: TRANSFER PORTAL CLOSES; SORSBY EXITS, LSU LANDS TOP CLASS
stories.body: The 2026 portal window shut with about 3,665 players in and 76% committed. Texas Tech QB Brendan Sorsby parted ways with the program, while Lane Kiffin's LSU assembled one of the cycle's top transfer classes.

deepDive.title: The Dot Plot as a Signaling Device
content: With the exchanges shuttered for Juneteenth, traders spent Friday re-reading the one document that actually moved this week: the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections. On Wednesday, Kevin Warsh's first meeting as Chair produced no change to the 3.50%-3.75% funds rate, yet the market still fell hard. The reason wasn't the rate itself but the dot plot - the grid of anonymous projections where 9 of 18 officials now see at least one hike in 2026 and the median quietly erased the cut investors had banked on. A piece of paper, not a transaction, set the tone.

The mechanism is expectations, not the overnight rate. Long-term asset prices discount the entire future path of short rates, so deleting a cut and adding hike risk lifts that path even when today's rate holds. That repricing showed up cleanly in the 2-year Treasury yield, which climbed toward 4.20% as the curve absorbed a higher policy floor. Equity valuations, which divide future cash flows by a discount rate built on those same expectations, compressed in response - the proximate driver of Wednesday's selloff before Thursday's partial bounce.

The dot plot has been a communication tool since 2012, introduced to make forward guidance transparent. The irony is that Warsh, before joining the Fed, spent years criticizing it as false precision that chains policymakers to forecasts they cannot keep. Markets treat the dots as a quasi-commitment; the Fed insists they are not promises. That tension has produced repeated whipsaws - 2018 and 2023 both saw projected paths abandoned within months - which is exactly why a single shift in the median dot can move trillions in a matter of minutes.

Bringing it back to this week: the same hawkish revision rippled across every line of the market strip above. The dollar firmed to a two-month high near 100.7, gold slipped toward $4,209 as real yields rose, and even oil's ~10% weekly slide reads partly as softer-demand pricing in a higher-rate world. None of it traded today, but Monday's reopen will test whether Thursday's relief rally was conviction or a holiday-thinned bounce. For a finance student, the lesson is durable: words from the Fed, properly priced, can hit harder than the rate decision itself.
